R034-01.notes: The sentence isolates the default as the only change, which rules out other causes of the participation jump. B, C and D have no support in the passage.

R034-02.notes: The context is that doing nothing is common, so whatever default is picked decides outcomes. A and C read in bias or self-interest the passage never mentions. D contradicts 'does not forbid anything.'

flags: minor: 'trained' and 'strengthened' are the physical-exercise traps but are weak. Few students would miss this one.
R034-03.notes: Freedom is exercised, meaning used, by busy people.

R034-04.notes: 'Less loudly' means it got less attention than the 'no one disputes' participation finding. 'Early studies also revealed' rules out A.

R034-05.notes: 'Not a flaw in the idea so much as the idea itself, seen from the other side.' Inertia is both why defaults work and why they hold people in place. D contradicts 'no one disputes.' B contradicts 'millions of accounts.'

R034-06.notes: The increases came out of future pay, so current take-home pay never dropped. B contradicts 'few later bothered to stop them,' which implies they could. C is absurd. The item is near the easy/medium border.

flags: minor: A describes the Passage A rule. It is a good reversal trap, but a careless reader may pick it.
R034-07.notes: Save More Tomorrow employees 'agreed in advance.' Under Passage A's rule, workers were enrolled with no action. B is the reverse of the passage (future pay). D is unsupported.

flags: minor: Passage A only implies that participation means more saving ('choosing it well can accomplish what years of reminders and lectures about saving could not'). The 'impression' is real but not stated. It is still defensible as the only option that B's contribution-rate discussion complicates.
minor: draws on the same 'saving less' evidence as R034-09; the two partially overlap.
R034-08.notes: B's evidence (workers stuck at low default rates, some saving less) undercuts the idea that higher participation means more saving. B explicitly concedes A ('no one disputes'). C concerns freedom, not contribution rates. B (the subgroup finding) is untouched.

flags: minor: key closely paraphrases B's sentence 'Some workers who would have joined on their own and chosen to save more ended up saving less,' so the item is close to a lookup.
R034-09.notes: B and D describe workers whom auto-enrollment helped (Passage A). A describes workers who escaped the default. C matches B's 'saving less' group.

passage_notes: Fact check: Passage A matches Madrian & Shea (2001). The firm switched to automatic enrollment in 1998. Participation was about 37% under opt-in vs. about 86% under automatic enrollment. Effects were largest for young and low-income workers. Most enrollees stayed at the 3% default and the money market fund default. Some would-be savers saved less. Passage B's program matches Thaler & Benartzi's Save More Tomorrow, where savings rose from about 3.5% to about 13.6% (more than tripled). No factual errors found. 'Fewer than half' and 'close to ninety percent' are fair roundings.
